title: From reactive to proactive: How diagnostic intelligence lowers avoidable utilization and lifts value-based performance
summary: Electronic health records integrations with genetic testing increases operational efficiency, enhances the provider experience and offers precision medicine at scale.
body_markdown:
Value-based care teams face many challenges:


- Rising inpatient and procedural costs
- Late identification of deteriorating chronic conditions
- Pressure to improve quality performance while controlling spend


For value-based care leaders, part of the cause for these challenges is due to claims-driven workflows surfacing risk too late when disease has already progressed and costly events have already occurred. Yet many healthcare leaders believe their existing claims analytics provide sufficient insight for[population health management](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/cultivate-stronger-population-health-outcomes-low-cost-interventions) .


However, claims data carries an inherent time lag—often 60 to 90 days—and captures only what’s already happened:


- The hospitalization
- The costly procedure
- The emergency room (ER) visit


Claims data is an inefficient and imprecise way to identify the gradual deterioration of kidney function, the progressive worsening of heart failure or the creeping elevation of hemoglobin A1c that precedes diabetic complications. **Diagnostic intelligence** —longitudinal[lab data paired with analytics](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/lab-data-missing-link-more-effective-chronic-disease-management-value-based-care-approach) —provides earlier clinical signals that:


- **Enable timely interventions**
- **Lead to fewer acute events**
- **Reduce avoidable hospitalizations**
- **Help organizations mitigate risk**
- **Improve quality performance and financial results**


Here’s how diagnostic intelligence accomplishes these feats.


## How lab data sees deterioration before claims arrive


Claims are lagging artifacts of encounters and coding. This means that adjudication delays and the absence of clinical values limit their utility for early detection. But lab results capture clinical information and biologic reality in near real-time and at high cadence.


For instance, the Kidney Health Evaluation for Patients with Diabetes (KED) measure requires both estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and a quantitative urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) to stage risk and guide therapy. However,[less than half of adults with diabetes](https://www.ncqa.org/report-cards/health-plans/state-of-health-care-quality-report/kidney-health-evaluation-for-patients-with-diabetes-ked/) receive this evaluation annually, leaving a large, addressable gap.


Even[modest reductions in eGFR](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2810033) or increases in albumin independently predict kidney failure, hospitalizations, heart failure and cardiovascular mortality—signals that arise months (and sometimes years) before a claim reflects deterioration.


Lab data can identify two eGFR measurements below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² that indicate chronic kidney disease (CKD) at a point when intervention can slow progression. A hemoglobin A1c of ≥6.5% confirms diabetes regardless of symptoms. Early screening using UACR can identify kidney disease long before manifestations become evident for patients—something claims data would miss entirely.


Heart failure behaves similarly. Rising natriuretic peptides (BNP/NTproBNP/ANP)[track with hospital admissions](https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/journal-scans/2014/04/07/15/37/changes-of-natriuretic-peptides-predict-hospital-admissions) in patients with chronic heart failure and[strongly predict rehospitalization.](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1161/JAHA.124.040320) Short term changes in peptide levels forecast near term admissions, reflecting an actionable early warning sign that lab data shows long before an inpatient claim posts.


Diagnostic data provides direct measurement of physiologic changes in real time. A B-type BNP level above 100 pg/mL or N-terminal pro-BNP above 210 pg/mL flags heart failure risk before hospitalization.


In diabetes, it’s not only the mean A1c that matters; the variability and trajectory of A1c over time are linked to[higher complications and mortality](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00592-020-01605-6) , making longitudinal lab history essential for risk stratification.


These thresholds detect disease long before claims-based algorithms identify the same patients. It’s also why plans that start the new member relationship with[“dayzero” historical lab data](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/day-zero-data-getting-pre-enrollment-insights-new-member-health) before the first in-network visit is recorded gain a critical head start on rising risk that’s otherwise invisible during the typical 60- to 90-day claims blackout.


## Real-world applications across chronic conditions


Integrating historical lab data into predictive models transforms early detection into targeted intervention. However, early detection only has an impact if it triggers specific, guideline concordant next steps that close the loop.


Consider three real-world pathways where diagnostic intelligence can reduce or prevent hospitalization and disease progression through actionable measures:


**Diabetes.** Quarterly A1c monitoring shows deteriorating control. In response, the care team intensifies treatment, addresses adherence barriers and provides self-management education. This leads to fewer ER visits and hospital admissions from complications.


**CKD.** Sequential eGFR measurements show progressive decline in a diabetic patient. The nephrologist responds by initiating SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, coordinating blood pressure optimization and providing nutrition counseling. With intervention, more patients avoid progression to dialysis or acute kidney injury requiring hospitalizations.


**Heart failure.** Routine monitoring reveals rising BNP levels. Using up-to-date lab data, care teams adjust diuretic therapy, schedule closer follow-ups and implement remote weight monitoring. This helps reduce future hospitalizations and ER visits that might have occurred without intervention.


The impact is measurable.


Crucially, when predictive identification is paired with proactive outreach, preventable utilization drops. Guided care management yielded a[27% reduction in potentially preventable admissions](https://www.ajmc.com/view/proactive-care-management-of-ai-identified-at-risk-patients-decreases-preventable-admissions) , demonstrating that risk targeted outreach can bend the inpatient curve.


Among Medicare Advantage (MA) members with congestive heart failure, analytics coupled with nurse outreach[reduced ER visits by 20%](https://ldi.upenn.edu/our-work/research-updates/the-effect-of-predictive-analytics-driven-interventions-on-healthcare-utilization/) and cardiology visits by 21% over a year, reinforcing how model driven care coordination can lower utilization.


MA members receiving value-based care had[24.3% fewer inpatient admissions](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/humana-report-finds-value-based-134500597.html?guccounter=1) than those in Original Medicare in 2024, along with 13.4% fewer ER visits. By 2025, MA enrollees in value-based arrangements experienced almost a[20% lower risk](https://www.interwellhealth.com/resources/insights/healthcare-utilization-trends-in-2025-how-health-plans-use-value-based-care-to-manage-costs) of acute hospitalizations and up to a 40% lower risk of 30-day readmissions.


Hispanic and Black MA beneficiaries experience[6%-12% lower rates](https://bettermedicarealliance.org/news/new-report-medicare-advantage-boosts-preventive-care-lowers-hospitalizations-for-seniors-across-populations/) of potentially avoidable hospitalizations when enrolled in value-based care programs, demonstrating how proactive identification reduces care disparities.


## Three benefits for health plans and organizations


### 1. Financial and quality performance improvements


Rebalancing spend from avoidable inpatient admissions to early outpatient management creates more headroom. For CKD alone, delaying dialysis ([often over $100,000 per patient per year)](https://www.goodrx.com/health-topic/kidneys/dialysis-cost) produces outsized ROI.


Simultaneously, better KED and glycemic control improves CMS Star Ratings and shared savings yields, while avoiding data submission friction, since value-based contracts increasingly tie reimbursement to quality and cost performance. MA plans achieving 4-star ratings receive[5% quality bonuses](https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=eeda99d4-aaaf-4981-acae-be264147e26c) , with an increase from 3 to 4 stars generating[$12-16.2 million](https://www.healthleadersmedia.com/strategy/one-star-improvement-can-increase-medicare-advantage-revenue-17) in additional revenue.


MA quality bonus payments[exceeded $12.7 billion in 2025](https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-advantage-quality-bonus-payments/) , and plans that lift quality performance gain bonus revenue and increased enrollment.


### 2. Risk adjustment factor (RAF) integrity


Risk adjustment accuracy represents another financial imperative. Lab results provide objective evidence to support diagnosis codes, supporting appropriate risk-based payments. For organizations operating under capitated or shared savings arrangements, preventing even a small number of hospitalizations generates substantial returns.


Lab testing can uncover uncoded or under-coded CKD and diabetes with complications, appropriately rightsizing baselines under CMSHCC changes.[In one large IPA](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/how-one-company-used-lab-data-insights-improve-population-management-chronic-kidney-disease-ckd) , Labcorp overlayed labs on claims data to reveal that approximately 80% of Stage 3 CKD patients had no CKD diagnosis on record, unlocking appropriate coding and earlier referral.


### 3. Improved operational efficiency


Successful programs don’t hand you raw data; instead, they deliver actionable lists by provider and patient, EHR embedded alerts and weekly activity files that your care teams can use. For example, Labcorp provides daily feeds and[Insight Analytics®](https://www.labcorp.com/data/insight-analytics) dashboards that unify our data on 50% of the U.S. population—including out-of-network results.


Our solutions integrate with over 700 EMR, PMS and LIS systems, serving as a single point of integration to provide a streamlined alternative to costly multi-EMR integrations, enriching existing workflows with actionable insights delivered at the point of care. Rather than replacing infrastructure, we enhance it by embedding alerts within EHRs through[Labcorp Diagnostic Assistant®](https://www.labcorp.com/data/diagnostic-assistant) and provide population-level dashboards through Insight Analytics, improving clinician satisfaction and patient outcomes.


Labcorp also offers at-home collection kits and access to over 2,200 patient service centers—located within a few miles of 95% of the U.S. population—to remove barriers from testing. Our payer/provider portals and HL7 feeds also support HEDIS submissions and real time kit/result tracking, making adoption practical rather than aspirational.


## Labcorp is your partner for diagnostic intelligence


As healthcare shifts toward value-based models, successful organizations will identify rising risk early and intervene effectively. Labcorp leverages insights from billions of lab results that allow healthcare organizations to:


- Identify high-risk patients earlier through lab intelligence
- Close gaps in care systematically with targeted interventions
- Improve coding accuracy and RAF capture with lab-validated risk profiles
- Expand access and equity through home collection and broad patient service center coverage


Diagnostic intelligence addresses the fundamental challenge of preventable hospitalizations by moving beyond retrospective claims analysis to real-time clinical intelligence. It provides the earliest signal that disease is progressing, allowing for targeted interventions to prevent costly acute events before they occur.
